power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: The everyday ecology of children's emotional experience Emotional experiences are fundamental inputs to human development, yet we know surprisingly little about their distribution in everyday life.
Research typically characterizes children's emotional environments using global reports or brief observations, obscuring the real-time contexts in which emotions arise.

Here, we used artificial intelligence to automatically transcribe and annotate daylong audio recordings from three samples totaling N=159 families with children aged 5 months-8 years old (48.43% female).

Our findings reveal the architecture of children's everyday emotional environments: positive speech was concentrated during play and music, and 25% of speech segments conveyed frustration, concentrated during routine caregiving.
Mothers' mental health did not predict affective speech, but lower child effortful control predicted more frustration in our toddler sample.
Frustration peaked in early toddlerhood, suggesting that children's growing independence at this age may reorganize family emotional environments.
Overall, emotional speech appears to emerge from everyday activity, with meaningful shifts across development.

Children's exposures to everyday emotions -including emotion words and emotional statements and expressions by caregivers, siblings, or peers -are thought to shape the foundations of lifelong mental health and wellbeing (LoBue & Ogren, 2022).
text.formatted: Children's exposures to everyday emotions -including emotion words and emotional statements and expressions by caregivers, siblings, or peers -are thought to shape the foundations of lifelong mental health and wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(LoBue & Ogren, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, we know surprisingly little about the everyday processes by which these experiences arise.

Theories of social emotional development state that the household emotional climate, including parents' expression of emotional states and their ability to manage their emotions to provide loving and supportive care -provides learning inputs for children's own abilities to regulate, key to adaptive responding to challenges throughout development (Morris et al., 2017; Sroufe et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Theories of social emotional development state that the household emotional climate, including parents' expression of emotional states and their ability to manage their emotions to provide loving and supportive care -provides learning inputs for children's own abilities to regulate, key to adaptive responding to challenges throughout development <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Morris et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Sroufe et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: One hypothesized mechanism by which family context can affect children's mental health is through repeated exposures to expressed emotions in everyday home environments (Morris et al., 2007).
text.formatted: One hypothesized mechanism by which family context can affect children's mental health is through repeated exposures to expressed emotions in everyday home environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Morris et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: For example, maternal anxiety has been associated with greater infant attention bias toward angry faces (Morales et al., 2017), whereas infants of mothers with depressive symptoms looked longer at happy than sad expressions, potentially reflecting greater familiarity with sadness (Hernandez-Reif et al., 2006).
text.formatted: For example, maternal anxiety has been associated with greater infant attention bias toward angry faces <ref type="bibr">(Morales et al., 2017)</ref>, whereas infants of mothers with depressive symptoms looked longer at happy than sad expressions, potentially reflecting greater familiarity with sadness <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hernandez-Reif et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Children's emotional exposure could arise through multiple pathways.
Emotion exposure may reflect relatively stable characteristics of family members -such as mothers' mental health or children's own temperament.
Emotional exposure might also arise from more dynamic features of everyday activities in which interactions unfold (Tamis-LeMonda & Masek, 2023).
text.formatted: Emotional exposure might also arise from more dynamic features of everyday activities in which interactions unfold <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Tamis-LeMonda & Masek, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Understanding the contributions of these different influences speaks to a central question about human behavior: to what extent do our experiences reflect more or less enduring dispositional traits, and how much do they dynamically fluctuate in response to the situations around us?
However, most of what we know about children's emotional environments uses parent reports or structured observations which cannot fully capture the processes that lead to emotional exposure.
Gold-standard video assessments provide unparalleled access to multimodal parent-child activity in high definition (Adolph, 2020).
text.formatted: Gold-standard video assessments provide unparalleled access to multimodal parent-child activity in high definition <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Adolph, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, because these assessments involve recording children and their parents for brief periods of time in researcher-structured circumstances, they cannot capture many of the everyday activities from which emotions may arise in real-world interactions.
Since emotions are inherently subjective, surveys that evaluate individuals' own experiences are arguably one of the most meaningful ways to assess emotions (Teoh et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Since emotions are inherently subjective, surveys that evaluate individuals' own experiences are arguably one of the most meaningful ways to assess emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Teoh et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, traditional surveys are not suited for capturing within-person variation in emotions over time (Shiffman et al., 2008).
text.formatted: However, traditional surveys are not suited for capturing within-person variation in emotions over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Shiffman et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Repeated sampling approaches, such as ecological momentary assessments, reveal that emotions shift dynamically throughout the day (Mehl et al., 2024; Reitsema et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Repeated sampling approaches, such as ecological momentary assessments, reveal that emotions shift dynamically throughout the day <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Mehl et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Reitsema et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, this type of assessment can only provide sporadic insight into emotional experiences and may therefore miss much of the richness of everyday emotional life, including fleeting but potentially important moments of affect.
Overall, past work in this area rarely captures the volume of highresolution data required to examine how emotions emerge through everyday activities and interactions.
Mobile and wearable sensors offer new opportunities to capture these processes in real time.

In the last decade, researchers have increasingly leveraged child-worn sensors to capture long stretches of children's everyday experiences in unconstrained, real-world settings (de Barbaro, 2019; Fausey et al., 2016; Franchak et al., 2024; Laudańska et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In the last decade, researchers have increasingly leveraged child-worn sensors to capture long stretches of children's everyday experiences in unconstrained, real-world settings (de <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Barbaro, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Fausey et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Franchak et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Laudańska et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In such studies, children may wear, for example, a lightweight audio recorder or head-mounted camera to capture what is in view -or earshot -of the child across the day, week, or month in real world settings.
Two related insights from this emerging field inform the current work.

First, expansive time, space, and responsibilities at home can change the ways that caregivers interact with their children at home relative to brief structured assessments (de Barbaro & Fausey, 2022).
text.formatted: First, expansive time, space, and responsibilities at home can change the ways that caregivers interact with their children at home relative to brief structured assessments (de <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Barbaro & Fausey, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For example, mothers are known to speak more to children in structured interactions than at home (Tamis-LeMonda et al., 2017), where they move more freely in and out of shared attention and proximity with their child over the day.
text.formatted: For example, mothers are known to speak more to children in structured interactions than at home <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Tamis-LeMonda et al., 2017)</ref>, where they move more freely in and out of shared attention and proximity with their child over the day.

text.text: Structured assessments can also bias children's emotional environments.
For example, up to 70% of infants do not show negative affect within free play sessions commonly used to study parent-child interactions (Leerkes et al., 2009; McElwain & Booth-LaForce, 2006).
text.formatted: For example, up to 70% of infants do not show negative affect within free play sessions commonly used to study parent-child interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Leerkes et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">McElwain & Booth-LaForce, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, maternal negative affect is rare during free play, occurring less than 1% of the time in one study (Somers & Luecken, 2022).
text.formatted: Similarly, maternal negative affect is rare during free play, occurring less than 1% of the time in one study <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Somers & Luecken, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In everyday settings, parents may sit down and play with their children, but they must also ensure that their child is dressed, fed, and ready for the day, while simultaneously caring for themselves and potentially other children.

These caregiving activities may challenge or frustrate children and their caregivers as they may require children to interrupt preferred activities, tolerate limits or delays, and comply with caregiver demands.
Second, parent and child behavior is dynamic and emerges in real time through everyday interactions.

For example, while most developmental research highlights the importance of between-person differences in language use to children's language development (Anderson et al., 2021), parents do not speak uniformly to their children across the day: rather, there are periods of time that there is lots of speech and other periods where there is less (Abney et al., 2017; Warlaumont et al., 2022; see also Abney et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, while most developmental research highlights the importance of between-person differences in language use to children's language development <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Anderson et al., 2021)</ref>, parents do not speak uniformly to their children across the day: rather, there are periods of time that there is lots of speech and other periods where there is less <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abney et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Warlaumont et al., 2022</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Abney et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: High-density sensor data can reveal the moment-to-moment predictors of speech within-person: by synchronizing audio recordings with cell phone screen logs, Mikhelson et al. (2024) recently revealed that periods of mothers' phone use at home were associated with 16% fewer words spoken around the child, relative to periods when the same mother was not on the phone.

(2024)</ref> recently revealed that periods of mothers' phone use at home were associated with 16% fewer words spoken around the child, relative to periods when the same mother was not on the phone.

text.text: Similarly, wearable audio recordings revealed that across the day, maternal sensitivity was highly variable within person, and that mothers were less sensitive during high-intensity emotional episodes, such as tantrumming siblings, relative to calmer occasions in the same families (de Barbaro & Madden-Rusnak, 2026).
text.formatted: Similarly, wearable audio recordings revealed that across the day, maternal sensitivity was highly variable within person, and that mothers were less sensitive during high-intensity emotional episodes, such as tantrumming siblings, relative to calmer occasions in the same families <ref type="bibr">(de Barbaro & Madden-Rusnak, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Such findings highlight the potential of longform wearable sensors to capture the dynamic within-person processes by which parent-child interactions -including everyday affect expressions -unfold at home.

Drawing from ecological frameworks of family emotional development, children's emotional exposures should also be shaped by more stable between-person regularities in children's and caregivers' characteristics and behavior (Morris et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Drawing from ecological frameworks of family emotional development, children's emotional exposures should also be shaped by more stable between-person regularities in children's and caregivers' characteristics and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Morris et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Children actively shape the flow of the interactions around them, including by eliciting feedback from caregivers.

Stable individual differences in children's temperament, or propensities for particular patterns of affect, attention and action, may therefore contribute to the emotional environments they experience.

For example, high levels of child negative affectivity, as well as low levels of effortful control, i.e. difficulties with regulating behavior and emotions, have been linked with greater parenting stress (Jańczak et al., 2025; Oddi et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For example, high levels of child negative affectivity, as well as low levels of effortful control, i.e. difficulties with regulating behavior and emotions, have been linked with greater parenting stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Jańczak et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Oddi et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, both child negative affectivity and surgency, i.e. high activity, impulsivity and approach behaviors, have been associated with greater parental distress, particularly in response to child negative emotion (Fields et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Additionally, both child negative affectivity and surgency, i.e. high activity, impulsivity and approach behaviors, have been associated with greater parental distress, particularly in response to child negative emotion <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fields et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Individual differences in parent mental health may also predict regularities in children's emotional exposures.

In structured interactions, depressed mothers exhibit more negative and less positive affect, are more withdrawn, and can be more irritable or prone to anger and conflict (Aktar & Bögels, 2017; Lovejoy et al., 2000).
text.formatted: In structured interactions, depressed mothers exhibit more negative and less positive affect, are more withdrawn, and can be more irritable or prone to anger and conflict <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Aktar & Bögels, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lovejoy et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Maternal anxiety is associated with more threat-focused parenting, including greater attention to danger and more fear-or threat-related communication in ambiguous or potentially threatening situations (Muris et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Maternal anxiety is associated with more threat-focused parenting, including greater attention to danger and more fear-or threat-related communication in ambiguous or potentially threatening situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Muris et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that maternal mental health may systematically shape the emotional content of children's everyday interactions.
Finally, children's emotional exposure may be distinct across developmental time periods.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial intelligence paired with longform child-worn audio recordings mean that we can now obtain unprecedented access into children's realworld emotional environments, including markers of the everyday activities from which individual emotional expressions arise in the moment.
Advances in automated transcription now allow speech within daylong audio recordings to be reliably transcribed at scale (Bain et al., 2023; Radford et al., 2023).

text.text: The current study leverages these tools to characterize the emotional content of speech produced by and around children in everyday home environments, regardless of speaker identity or whether speech is directed towards the child.

We examine how children's exposure to different emotions is distributed across the day, and the extent to which children's emotional exposures are predicted by relatively stable characteristics of parents and their children versus emerging dynamically in the moment from activity contexts.
We had three main hypotheses: 1) Children's emotional exposures will dynamically fluctuate across the day and be predicted by ongoing everyday activities in real time.
2) Children high in negative affectivity and surgency, and those low in effortful control/regulation will experience higher rates of negative affect in everyday speech.

3) Children of mothers with high anxiety symptoms will experience higher rates of fear-talk in everyday interactions and children of mothers with high depression symptoms will experience higher rates of sad-talk in everyday speech.

By examining these questions in three cross-sectional datasets ranging from infancy to middle childhood, we also observed the extent to which the organization of children's emotional environments differs across the first 8 years of life.

We analyzed full-day child-worn LENA audio recordings, collected in everyday realworld environments, from 159 participants across three comparable samples, with participants aged 5-11 months ("infants", n=70), 6 months -3.5 years (92.2% over 12 months old; "toddlers", n=51), and 3-8 years ("children", n=38; see also SM1).

Speech content present in each participants' audio recording was transcribed by WhisperX (Bain et al., 2023; Radford et al., 2023) and segmented into 30-second bins, which were then automatically annotated using GPT4.1mini (OpenAI, 2025) for everyday household activities and five categories of emotion, including enjoyment, frustration, anger, fear and sadness.

text.text: To protect participant privacy, we used only secure enterprise software or software that could be run on secure servers managed by UT Austin.

LENA audio recording duration totaled 3196.66 hours, with a mean of 20.10 hours recorded per participating family (SD = 6.66; median = 24.00; range = 1.24-24.04 hours), and 70.44% (112/159) of recordings over 21 hours (see SM2).
After segmenting and transcription, we identified 167,742 distinct 30-second bins containing speech across the 159 participants, covering 43.73% of the total recording duration.
Considering all segments containing speech, affect was detected in 40.36% of bins and activity was detected in 29.38% of bins (see SM3 for sample specific statistics).

Across the 167,742 30-second bins containing speech collected from all 159 children, frustration was the emotion most commonly detected in everyday speech, occurring in 25.65% bins, followed by enjoyment (12.66%).
Sadness, fear, and anger each appeared in fewer than 1.5% of coded bins.

This pattern replicated across our three age groups, with frustrated speech detected in 22.19% of coded bins in the infant sample, 28.68% in the toddler sample, and 26.96% in the child sample, followed by enjoyment (detected in 14.23%, 9.96%, and 14.44% of speech bins, respectively).
Frustration was also the most commonly detected emotion in 139 of 159 (87.42%) participants (IQR = 20.07-30.20%).

Caregiving routines (7.60%) and play (6.88%) were the two most commonly detected activities in our recordings, occurring at similar rates in the combined sample, with other activities, including mealtimes (4.65%), music/singing (1.8%), and media (1.7%) occurring less frequently in speech bins.
This overall pattern of detected activity was similar across samples.

We also discovered positive within-child associations between music/singing and enjoyment in all three samples, and lower within-child odds of frustration during play (see SM6).
We found relatively few correlations between emotional speech and parent and child characteristics (SM7).
Rates of negative affect in speech were not associated with child negative affectivity or surgency in any of our three samples.
However, in our toddler sample, children with lower regulation scores were exposed to more negative emotional speech (r = -.407, p = .0229).

Given that frustration accounted for the majority of negative affect, and was particularly prevalent during routine caregiving activities, we conducted an exploratory analysis examining child regulation specifically in relation to frustrated speech.

Toddlers with lower regulation were exposed to significantly more frustrated speech (r = -.428, p = .0164), consistent with the possibility that children's emerging regulatory capacities help shape the emotional interactions occurring around them.

However, the broader negative-affect association was not significant for toddlers following the Benjamini-Hochberg corrections for nine tested correlations (BH q = .206) and was not observed in our infant or child samples.
The frustration-specific finding was exploratory and requires independent replication.

text.text: We found no significant differences in the rates of anger or sadness between our samples.
However, fear-coded bins were significantly more frequent in the child sample (1.62%) than in the infant (1.00%) and toddler samples (1.08%).
Next, we found significantly higher rates of play detected in the child sample (12.08%) relative to play in the infant and toddler samples (5.21% and 5.05%, respectively).
Rates of enjoyment, however, were matched between the infant and the child samples (13.88% and 14.25%, respectively), which both had significantly higher enjoyment than the toddler sample (9.74%).
Finally, media and reading were more frequent in the child sample relative to infant and toddler samples, and speech about sleep was most common in the infant sample (see SM8 for full statistics).
The current study examined everyday emotional speech in thousands of hours of childworn audio recordings drawn from 159 children spanning five months to 8 years of age.
Our findings reveal that affect is pervasive in everyday speech, and that children's emotional environments have a rich ecological structure.
Different emotions have vastly different base rates of expression, with frustration and enjoyment by far the most common in everyday home interactions.

We found limited associations between children's emotional environments and relatively stable characteristics of family members, alongside strong evidence that emotional expression was tied to families' activity in the moment.
These patterns were broadly similar from infancy to school age, speaking to their generalization across the wide variation in developmental stages.
At the same time, we observed key areas of distinction between samples, suggesting children inhabit distinct emotional ecologies across ages.
Approximately 18% of all thirty-second recorded segments included a spoken expression of emotion, including both overnight periods and silence.
In segments with speech, children experienced high levels of frustration (25.65% of bins) and enjoyment (12.66% of bins), with substantially fewer expressions of anger, sadness, and fear.

These findings contrast with past work which has generally found that children's exposure to markers of emotion is relatively rare in real-world interactions (Hoemann et al., 2026; Ogren & Sandhofer, 2021), and that positive emotions are much more likely to be expressed than negative emotions in both structured and unstructured parent-child interactions (Jackson & Geangu, 2026; Somers & Luecken, 2022).

text.text: Two main differences between our work and past studies are likely to account for these discrepancies.

First, past studies of real-world emotional exposure have examined the use of explicit emotion labels (e.g. happy, sad, frustrated; Nencheva et al., 2023; Ogren & Sandhofer, 2021), or facial expressions in view of infants (Hoemann et al., 2026; Jackson & Geangu, 2026; Palmer et al., 2026).

text.text: However, neither parents nor children label each emotion that they express, meaning that emotion labels are likely an undercount of emotion expression in speech (Nencheva et al., 2023).

text.text: Similarly, faces are not often in view of young children (Deak et al., 2014; Fausey et al., 2016) and thus observed facial expressions may simply not provide a high volume of emotional exposure for children.

text.text: By leveraging a large language model to detect more subtle linguistic expressions of emotions in parent and child speech, we observed emotional content not captured by prior studies.

More broadly, given that sound can be heard irrespective of where a child is looking, auditory signals may provide children more pervasive access to ongoing emotional information in their environments.
Indeed, sounds -via words and/or tonesmay alert children to orient to faces at key moments, a behavioral pathway that may be critical for supporting learning about emotional facial expressions.
Second, many past studies of parent-child emotion draw from researcher-constrained recordings of dyadic interactions, including structured free play sessions.

There is a long practice of capturing "unstructured" home interactions in developmental psychology, ranging from 1-2 hours to full day or overnight recordings (Ainsworth et al., 1978; Schuengel et al., 1999; Soska et al., 2021; J. Sullivan et al., 2021; Teti et al., 2010).

text.text: However, a number of considerations are likely to affect the nature of emotional expression in such recordings.
First, relative to recordings captured remotely, the presence of researchers can decrease the insensitivity of parent child interactions (Lee et al., 2017).
text.formatted: First, relative to recordings captured remotely, the presence of researchers can decrease the insensitivity of parent child interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Lee et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Next, the absence of other family members may change interactions at home, including for example, decreasing sibling conflict, a common source of frustration and prohibitions.
Finally, recordings may differ in the extent to which they capture routine caregiving activities, major contextual drivers of expressed frustration in our sample.

Semi-structured observations of mealtimes, bedtimes, and clothing or diaper changes (Jian & Teti, 2016; Maas et al., 2013; Messina et al., 2020; Saltzman et al., 2018) indicate that these may provide developmentally meaningful access to variation in frustration, hostility, and parenting insensitivity more broadly.

text.text: The emotional speech captured in our sample likely reflects a combination of these factors, highlighting the unique potential of daylong recordings of real-world interactions to capture a representative sample of everyday family activity.
Next, we observed that emotions were structured dynamically by ongoing activities occurring around the children.
Enjoyment was more likely to appear during play and singing.
Frustrated speech was much more likely to appear during mealtimes and other routine caregiving tasks including bathing, dressing and getting out of the house.
In post-hoc analyses, we further determined that frustration often emerged during prohibitions or conflict between family members (SM9).

Where much past work has examined emotional expression as a relatively stable characteristic of parents or children, this work indicates that everyday activities are a potent dynamic organizer of children's real-world emotional experiences.

Our findings are more consistent with work leveraging high-density survey designs like EMA which document dynamic fluctuations in emotions across the day (Nencheva et al., 2026; Reitsema et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Our findings are more consistent with work leveraging high-density survey designs like EMA which document dynamic fluctuations in emotions across the day <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Nencheva et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Reitsema et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, EMA surveys require active response by participants, which means that even on the high end they are relatively sparse, ranging from 8-15 reports per day.

By instead annotating emotional speech from continuous audio recordings, we were able to gain access to thousands of datapoints per day from each participant -approximately two orders of magnitude more data on emotional expression than EMA studies can provide.

These high-density annotations provided access to repeated instances of emotional expression paired with ongoing activities at scale, allowing us to observe the dynamic structure by which emotions emerged over the course of the day.

The high volumes of frustration observed in our samples -with 75% of children experiencing frustration in at least one in five speech-containing bins-suggest that this is a relatively normative dimension of young children's emotional environments in North American families.
The developmental implications of this will require longitudinal samples.

However, while past work has linked parent hostility with worse child outcomes (Pinquart, 2017; Polcari et al., 2014), the pervasiveness of frustration in our sample means it is unlikely that frustration alone is an indication of maladaptive family dynamics.

text.text: Critically, our annotations distinguished between speech containing frustration versus anger, where frustration included speech indicating annoyance, irritation or impatience, whereas anger codes required hostility, aggression or rejection.
And although exposure to frustration was pervasive, exposure to anger was relatively rare: accounting for 0.15%-0.63% of bins for 75% of all families.

Most broadly, these findings suggest that the context of observation may change the behaviors we observe: in relatively brief, "minimally" structured interactions where researchers are present, even behaviors that are relatively common at home may be substantially less likely to surface.

This may be particularly relevant for studies of emotion or social emotional development, where caregivers' responses to challenging or distressful situations are often more predictive of attachment security and childhood outcomes than their responses in neutral contexts (Leerkes et al., 2009; McElwain & Booth-LaForce, 2006).

text.text: Third, several findings were suggestive of developmental effects.
First, we observed the least amount of frustrated speech in our infant sample, with significantly higher frustration in both our toddler and child samples, appearing to peak during toddlerhood.

This is consistent with past work linking the onset of infant locomotion to increases in parental frustration and prohibitions in self-report and structured observations (Biringen et al., 1995; Campos et al., 1992; Zumbahlen & Crawley, 1996).

text.text: However, to our knowledge this is the first time that large-scale daylong recordings have been used to demonstrate an increase in frustration with toddlers relative to infants.
Interestingly, we also observed relatively high amounts of enjoyment in our infant sample, suggesting something of a "honeymoon" period at this age.
By contrast, enjoyment was lowest in our toddler sample before rebounding in the child sample.

Broadly, these findings are consistent with the idea that children's growing independence, activity, self-regulation and family responsibilities change, so do the distributions of emotions that children encounter (Campos et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Broadly, these findings are consistent with the idea that children's growing independence, activity, self-regulation and family responsibilities change, so do the distributions of emotions that children encounter <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Campos et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: However, given that our three samples were collected independently and age and sample were confounded, the possibility remains that these differences reflect sampling differences rather than age differences per se.
Finally, relatively stable characteristics of mothers and children made more limited contributions to children's emotional environments.
In our toddler sample only, lower effortful control predicted a higher rate of frustrated speech.
Frustrated speech often contained prohibitions, likely from caregivers (SM9).

However, following replication in other samples, future work should attempt to distinguish different potential sources of this speech -including from caregivers, the child's own speech, or the speech of other nearby children -to pinpoint how and why these increases in frustrated speech may emerge at this age.
The association between regulation and frustrated speech did not generalize to infants or older children.
However, heightened issues around compliance in toddlerhood may highlight individual differences in self-regulation.
These issues may be less salient in infancy, where autonomy is still limited, and with older children, as they gain communication skills and autonomy, for example.

Consistent with this, survey research has documented challenges with child compliance and tantrumming typically begin around 12 months, peaking between 18-24 months (Potegal & Davidson, 2003; M. W. Sullivan & Lewis, 2012).

text.text: We saw no significant relationships between mothers' anxiety or depression symptoms and children's affective environments.
Future efforts to isolate maternal speech input in the recording may reveal additional associations.
For example, our human coders identified that media was a common source of fear talk in many families, likely contributing noise to associations with maternal mental health.
We did not attempt to distinguish sources of emotional speech input in the current work, as media can and should be considered a valid source of children's emotional input in real-world environments.

However, examining the emotional content of maternal speech may be particularly useful when considering mothers speech input as a potential behavioral pathway of intergenerational transmission of depression and anxiety symptoms (LoBue & Ogren, 2022).

text.text: We acknowledge several limitations.

First, we used transcripts from child-worn audio recordings to characterize children's emotional exposures, meaning emotions expressed through vocal tone, facial expression, or other bodily signals were not captured by our approach.
Recent work confirms that speech content conveys much meaningful information about affect (Koch et al., 2026; Wolf et al., 2023).

text.text: However, multimodal emotional signals may change the meaning of speech content, for example when someone speaks sarcastically (Yadavalli et al., 2026).

text.text: Similarly, while speech often accompanies activity, some activities are done silently, and other times, speech about a given activity does not signify that that an activity is occurring in the moment.
As such our activities should be interpreted as not referring to observed activities per se but rather speech suggesting the probability of an activity.

More broadly, while AI transcription and annotation have substantially improved in recent years, AI recall rates were not high across all emotion categories and human-AI reliability was somewhat lower than gold-standard human-human annotation (Kappa = .8; Bakeman & Gottman, 1997) for some annotations, although not out of the range of acceptability.

text.text: Next, our analyses do not account for who was expressing detected affect.

As such, expressed emotions combine those expressed by parents or other caregivers with those expressed by the target child and any other children or other individuals in range of the LENA audio recordings.
Future work should attempt to distinguish these different potential sources of children's emotional inputs.

Finally, while leveraging data from three samples allowed us to examine generalization of emotional environments and their organization across developmental periods, the fact that our samples were recruited independently means that sample is confounded with age change and we do not have clean age comparisons.

We note that all data was collected in Austin, and sample demographics across the three groups was largely similar, although education and income were highest for our oldest sample, which was also whiter than our other samples.
As such, observed distinctions across ages should be examined in additional samples that can better control for such differences in future work.
Together, our findings reveal that children's everyday emotional environments are systematically organized around day-to-day family activities.
Frustration was a common feature of everyday speech, particularly during caregiving routines, while positive emotional speech was concentrated during play and music.
Differences across developmental samples further suggest that these environments reflect the changing demands of childhood.
By documenting emotional exposures as they unfold in realworld settings, this work provides a foundation for understanding how everyday emotional experiences contribute to children's development.

The current study included N= 159 total children aged 5 months to 8 years, drawn from three independent samples each including child-worn audio recordings, child temperament and parent mental health measures.

Our infant sample was collected between 2025-2026 and included N=70 families from the BABYConnect Study, an ongoing longitudinal study with 24-hour audio recordings with infants aged 5-11 months (M=7.6, SD=1.0).

Our toddler sample was collected beginning in 2022 with the ongoing Whole Communities Whole Health Project and included N=51 families with a child aged between 7 months to 3.5 years old (M= 2.0, SD=0.8; 47/51 or 92.2% of target children were over 12 months old).
Our child sample was collected from 2024-2026 as part of the Caregiver-Child Dynamics and Socioemotional Development Study and included N=38 families with a child aged 3-8 years old (M=5.6, SD=1.3).
All study procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of Texas at Austin.
Written informed consent was obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all participating children.
Demographics and eligibility criteria were unique to each sample.
Full demographic information is available in Supplemental Materials SM1.
Infant Sample (BABYConnect; IRB#: STUDY00005017).

Infant sample participants (n=70) were drawn from the BABYConnect (Building Bonds with Your Baby through Everyday Connections) project, an ongoing longitudinal study following 140 mothers from the third trimester to 18 months postpartum.
Mothers were recruited during pregnancy from the Austin metropolitan area from a maternal-fetal medicine clinic and Facebook advertisements.

Eligibility criteria included planning to speak Spanish, English, or both languages to their children; not being pregnant with multiples; and the infant being expected to be home without medical assistance by 6 months postpartum.
All participating families who shared LENA audio by July 31, 2026 were included in the current analyses.
Infants in this sample ranged from 5.0-11.1 months old (M= 7.6, SD=1.0), with most being 6-8 months old, see age histogram S1); 42.9% were female.
Mothers were predominantly non-Hispanic White (52.2%) and Hispanic (35.8%) with the remainder being Black (6%), Asian (3%), or multiracial (3%).
79.1% of included mothers primarily spoke English and 20.9% spoke Spanish.

The sample had a diversity of income levels, with 29.8% reporting earning less than $50,000 a year, 19.4% between $50,000 and $100,000, 25.4% between $100,000 and $200,000 and 25.4% greater than $200,000.
Mothers ranged in age from 20 to 48 (mean = 33).
Toddler Sample (WCWH Study; IRB#: STUDY00001345).
Toddler participants (N=51) were drawn from the Whole Communities-Whole Health (WCWH) project, a five-year, community-engaged longitudinal cohort study of 497 participants.
Families were recruited from the east-central Greater Austin area.
Eligibility criteria included having a child younger than 4 and living in or near the Del Valle area of East Austin, Texas.

Inclusion in the current study required families to record and share at least 3 hours of LENA audio and complete the Mood and Anxiety Symptom Questionnaire (MASQ) to assess caregiver depression and anxiety symptoms.
Children averaged 2.01 years of age (SD = 0.76), with 92.2% of children (47/51) being older than 1 year; 51.0% were female.
Among caregivers with available race/ethnicity data (n = 40), 20.0% were White, 57.5% Hispanic, 15.0% Black, 2.5% Asian, and 5.0% multiracial.
Among the 43 caregivers with survey-language data, 65.1% completed the survey in English and 34.9% in Spanish.

Based on reported annual household-income categories (n = 42), 31.0% reported incomes below $50,000, 11.9% reported $50,000-$99,999, 47.6% reported $100,000-$199,999, and 9.5% reported $200,000 or more.
Among caregivers with valid age data (n = 39), age ranged from 23-43 years (mean = 32.69).

Protocols varied across samples, however in all samples families were instructed to collect and share a 24-hour LENA (Language ENvironment Analysis) home audio recording and to complete survey measures including family demographics, child temperament, and maternal depression and anxiety symptom questionnaires.
As surveys were not necessarily completed at the same time as the LENA recordings (detailed below), we report child age at the time of the LENA recording for each sample.
In the BABYConnect study, LENA audio recordings were collected following a home visit occurring when infants were approximately 6-8 months of age.

Mothers completed questionnaires as part of the longitudinal study, including demographic characteristics (57 prenatally, 13 postnatally, 0.4-5.2 months, M = 1.7 month of age), mental health symptoms (5.78-10.41 months of age, M = 7.64), and infant temperament (.5-7.3 months of age, M = 2.41).
The mean time between the LENA recording and child temperament measure was 5.69 months (SD = 1.71, range = 0.95-9.43; n = 50).
Two children were excluded from the temperament analyses because they completed their assessments very early in infancy, at 10 and 14 days after birth.
The mean time between the LENA recording and maternal depression and anxiety symptom surveys was 0.22 months (SD = 0.28, range = 0-1.74; n = 65).
In the WCWH longitudinal cohort study, families collected waves of data for up to five years during their participation in the study.

These data included daylong LENA audio recordings twice per year and surveys relating to parent and child characteristics, including child temperament and maternal mental health, also occurring twice per year.
While surveys and LENA recordings were both collected at biannual assessment waves, they were not completed concurrently.
For the current study, for each child we selected the longest recording.
Then, we matched the LENA recording to the temperament and mental health measurement completed closest to the recording date.
We prioritized measurements within 6 months before or after the recording date.
If no questionnaire was collected within this time window, we selected the closest available assessment.
The mean time between the LENA recording and child temperament measure was 7.20 months (SD = 5.36, range = 0.72 -21.55, n = 32, range).

The corresponding intervals for maternal depression and anxiety symptom assessments were 5.80 months (SD = 4.53, range = 1.05-21.03; n = 46) and 5.83 months (SD = 4.58, range = 1.05-21.03; n = 45), respectively.
In the CDSD study, caregiver-child dyads participated in laboratorybased longitudinal study with 4 waves, each 6 months apart.
At wave 1, demographic information, standardized measures of maternal mental health and child temperament were collected online a few days prior to an in-person laboratory visit.
Families received the LENA audio recorder during the laboratory visit and had two weeks to complete their recording.

The mean time between the LENA recording and child temperament measure was 0.75 months (SD = 0.70, range = 0.10-3.58; n = 31) for the child temperament analysis and 0.73 months (SD = 0.65, range = 0.10-3.58; n = 38) for both the maternal depression and anxiety symptom analyses.
Across the three samples, all participating children wore a LENA recording device during one full day in their natural home environments.
Caregivers were provided the same recording instructions across all three samples.

Specifically, caregivers were instructed to turn on the recorder within one hour of waking up and keep it on throughout the recording period, allowing children to engage in their usual activities throughout the day.
The target recording duration was 24 hours per family.

To protect participants' privacy and autonomy, families were also instructed that they could pause or stop the recorder at any time for any amount of time, and that they could choose to delete all or any part of the recording after they had completed recordings.
The recorder was worn by children in a pocket on a vest provided by the study team.
Caregivers were allowed to remove the device as needed for activities in which wearing the recorder was not appropriate.
After recording, the audio files were saved locally, uploaded to the LENA system for processing, and subsequently deleted from LENA storage in accordance with individual study IRB protocols.

The mean LENA recording duration was M = 18.29 hours, SD =7.71, range = 1.24-24.04 hours for our infant sample, M = 22.20 hours, SD = 4.57, range = 3.04-24.01 hours for our toddler sample, and M = 20.96 h, SD = 5.51 h, range = 6.73 -24 for our child sample.
Each sample collected different measures of maternal mental health.
For the infant sample, mothers were assessed for postpartum and anxiety symptoms with the Edinburg Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS; Cox et al., 1996) and the GAD-7 (Spitzer et al., 2006).

The IBQ (Putnam et al., 2014) is a 37-item measure of infant temperament.

Transcription.
Raw audio files from LENA were processed through a multi-step WhisperX (Bain et al., 2023; Radford et al., 2023) transcription pipeline.
text.formatted: Raw audio files from LENA were processed through a multi-step WhisperX <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bain et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Radford et al., 2023)</ref> transcription pipeline.

text.text: First, recordings were saved as WAV audio files and then divided into 5-second segments and transcribed using WhisperX version 3.7.4.
The transcription pipeline included voice activity detection, automatic transcription, and time alignment.
The resulting data included segment start time, segment end time, and transcribed text for each segment.

Transcripts were cleaned by removing or redacting personally identifiable and sensitive information, including names, locations, workplaces, and other real-world identifying details, and replacing such information with "***".
To balance temporal precision with sufficient contextual information within each segment, 5-second segments were grouped to create 30-second segments.

After processing, the final dataset included 167,742 valid 30-second transcript segments across 159 families: 70 in the infant sample, 51 in the toddler sample, and 38 in the child sample, which we combined into 30-second bins in order to provide our annotation model additional context for making emotion and activity judgements.
Transcription Accuracy.

English-language transcription quality was evaluated against ground-truth human reference transcripts for 75 30-second segments randomly selected from five daylong recordings in the FauseyTrio HomeBank corpus (Fausey & Mendoza, 2018).

text.text: Median unigram precision was 82.8%, with median bigram, trigram, and 4-gram precision of 67.7%, 57.1%, and 47.6%, respectively, indicating substantial overlap between the words produced by WhisperX and those in the human reference texts.
Recall was lower, with median unigram, bigram, trigram, and 4-gram recall of 54.5%, 40.0%, 34.8%, and 28.1%, respectively.
Mean word error rate was 60.9%, and automated transcripts averaged 69.4% of reference length.

Overall, this pattern of results indicates that while the automated transcription produced text that was generally reliable, it also systematically missed a portion of what was said on the recording, indicating non-trivial errors and omissions.
Human review of segments with relatively low recall values indicated that this was often related to quieter speech or speech in the background of the recording.
Spanish-language transcription quality was evaluated against ground-truth humanreference transcripts for 150 segments 30-second segments.
Segments were randomly selected from transcripts of nine Spanish speaking participants from the BABYConnect study.
Two native Spanish speakers each transcribed the segments independently and then collaboratively conferenced their transcriptions to create the ground truth sample.

Median unigram precision was 64.5%, with median bigram, trigram, and 4-gram precision of 37.8%, 20.0%, and 8.6%, respectively, indicating moderate overlap between the words produced by WhisperX and those in the human reference texts that declined sharply for longer word sequences.
Recall was lower, with median unigram, bigram, trigram, and 4-gram recall of 45.9%, 26.7%, 14.7%, and 8.0%, respectively.
Mean word error rate was 64.7%, and automated transcripts averaged 75.2% of reference length.

Overall, this pattern of results indicates that Spanish-language transcription was somewhat lower quality than English-language transcription and that while the automated transcription captured many individual words it also missed or altered some portion of what was said, particularly in multiword sequences.

ChatGPT-based annotation was used to identify affect and activity from each transcript segment using UT Austin's Enterprise Technology, which has a variety of data protections, including limited data retention periods, local university administration, and by default not using inputs to train models.

Combined with our PII removal pipeline, this allowed us to leverage ChatGPT functionality while also maintaining control of participant's data, protecting their privacy, and preventing their data from being used by for-profit companies.

The model received the segmented transcript generated by the WhisperX transcription pipeline together with a structured prompt that included instructions for identifying affect and activity based on linguistic information in the transcript.

Dictionary-based methods, including for example LIWC (Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010) and the lexicon-based tools in the syuzhet R package (Jockers, 2015; H. Kim, 2022), estimate affect by matching text to a list of predefined emotion or sentiment words.

text.text: These approaches have difficulty distinguishing meanings that depend on context.
For example, a dictionary that includes "hot" as a synonym for anger could misclassify a reference to "Hot Wheels" as emotional language.

Contextual encoder models such as BERT represent an advance by interpreting words in relation to surrounding text, with classification typically accomplished through fine-tuning on labeled examples (Devlin et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Contextual encoder models such as BERT represent an advance by interpreting words in relation to surrounding text, with classification typically accomplished through fine-tuning on labeled examples <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Devlin et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Instructionfollowing generative LLMs, such as those underlying ChatGPT, extend these capabilities by applying detailed coding instructions directly to passages and drawing on learned knowledge of situations and relationships to interpret implied meaning.
Their value for emotional language analysis lies in identifying what speakers communicate through an exchange, including emotions that are never explicitly named.
Evidence supports both the interpretive capacity of these models and their effectiveness for large-scale annotation.

GPT models have outperformed dictionary-based approaches in psychological text analysis and fine-tuned BERT-based classifiers on some implicit-emotion recognition tasks (Boutouta et al., 2025; Rathje et al., 2024).

text.text: When given the same coding instructions, ChatGPT also classified tweets and news articles more accurately than crowd workers-by approximately 25 percentage points on average across four datasets-and produced greater agreement across repeated annotations at substantially lower cost (Gilardi et al., 2023).

text.text: This combination of contextual interpretation and scalable annotation is especially valuable for studying children's emotional language environments.
A parent's statement, "Stop that-I've already told you five times to stop," can communicate frustration without containing an explicit emotion word.

LLM-assisted analysis offers a way to capture these indirect expressions systematically across extensive recordings, expanding measurement from the emotional vocabulary children hear to the emotional meaning conveyed in everyday speech.

To obtain automated affect and activity annotations, we submitted each 30-second transcript segment to OpenAI's GPT-4.1 mini model using a Python script to automate API requests, accessing GPT through the university's secure enterprise AI service.

For each segment, the prompt provided detailed instructions as to our coding scheme and instructed the model to consider explicit linguistic cues as well as the surrounding conversational context within each segment.
When there was insufficient linguistic or contextual evidence to make a reliable classification, the model was instructed to assign an NA label.
The model was also instructed to provide an evidence note documenting the basis for the classification or the lack of sufficient evidence.
We share our script, including complete coding prompts, derived from a publicly available script by Rathje et al. (2024) in SM 13.
text.formatted: We share our script, including complete coding prompts, derived from a publicly available script by <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Rathje et al. (2024)</ref> in SM 13.

text.text: To assess the reliability of automated GPT annotations, we trained human research assistants on both activity and affect coding schemes.
Following training, subsets of transcript segments were selected for human annotation.
Initial assessments revealed that certain affect categories appeared rarely, meaning selected transcripts were highly skewed containing few examples of each affect or activity category.
Thus, to increase the robustness of our reliability values we used GPT predictions for each category to randomly select segments that contained positive predictions.
For each emotion or activity category in each set, the reliability subsets contained 50% positive predictions from GPT randomly shuffled with 50% randomly selected segments from the database.
Human coders were blind to GPT predictions.
We used between 40-60 transcribed 30-second segments for each category of emotion or activity.

Reliability segments were independently coded by 2-3 trained human annotators with final scores representing average performance 1) among all human coders and 2) between each human coder and our GPT model.

In keeping with the gold standards within each field, human-human reliability was evaluated using Cohen's Kappa and ChatGPT-Human reliability was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 score, balanced accuracy, and Cohen's kappa.

For both affect and activity, both human coders and GPT were instructed to use a threepoint scale in which 0 indicated that the target affect or activity was absent, 1 indicated mild confidence that the target affect or activity present (i.e. that it was likely), and 2 indicated strong confidence that the target affect or activity was present.
For all reliability calculations and analyses, we binarized each rating (0 = absent; scores ≥1 = present; except for anger/frustration, see below), as detailed below.
Complete reliability values for human-human and human-GPT are presented in SM11.
Affect coding.

Using the script described above, we prompted ChatGPT to annotate five categories of emotion spanning two broad dimensions of affect: Positive affect, i.e. enjoyment, and negative affect, including fear, frustration, anger and sadness.
Initially, each emotion was coded on a three-point scale and frustration and anger were not differentiated.
However, early results indicating large volumes of predicted frustration/anger prompted us to further distinguish these.
In our final coding scheme, frustration and anger are derived from a five-point scale, where 0 indicated no detected frustration/anger, 1-2 indicated frustration, and 3-4 indicated anger.
Each affect category was evaluated independently, allowing multiple emotions to cooccur within a single 30-second segment.
Ratings captured both explicit references to emotions and indirect linguistic expressions of affect, interpreted within the surrounding conversational context.
References to emotions experienced by others, hypothetical situations, and media content could also be coded.
However, isolated emotion words or situations that might reasonably elicit emotion were not sufficient without relevant emotional meaning in context.
Ambiguous but meaningful evidence of affect could receive a lower intensity score.
When multiple expressions of the same affect occurred within a segment, the highest supported intensity was assigned rather than averaging across expressions.

Across human-human rating pairs, Cohen's kappa for the 30-second reliability segments was .795 for enjoyment, .599 for frustration/anger, .667 for sadness, and .800 for fear, indicating acceptable agreement between our human coders.

Among human-GPT precision was .792 for enjoyment, .852 for frustration/anger, .867 for sadness, and .848 for fear, and recall was .760 for enjoyment, .821 for frustration/anger, .788 for sadness, and .875 for fear for the 30-second reliability segments and (see SM 10 for complete table).

Moderate-to-high precision combined with very high recall for enjoyment and frustration/anger indicates that GPT identified nearly all human-coded instances of these emotions, although some positive predictions were not confirmed by human coders.

In contrast, higher precision but substantially lower recall for sadness and fear indicates that GPT's positive classifications were generally consistent with human judgments, but it failed to identify approximately half of the instances identified by human coders.
Enjoyment.
Enjoyment encompassed expressions of happiness, pleasure, amusement, affection, excitement, and delight.
Speech was rated on a 0-2 scale:0 = no enjoyment,1 = possible or mild enjoyment, and2 = clear enjoyment.
Evidence included explicit positive emotion language, affectionate expressions, celebration, and enthusiastic engagement in enjoyable activities.

Routine politeness, praise, positive conversational content, or formulaic expressions of affection (e.g., "love you, bye" at the end of a phone call) were not sufficient without additional contextual evidence of enjoyment.
Frustration and anger were coded along a shared angerrelated affective continuum, ranging from mild annoyance and irritation to explicit anger and hostility.
Speech was rated on a 0-4 scale:0 = no frustration or anger,1 = possible frustration,2 = clear frustration or irritation,3 = clear anger, and4 = strong or escalated anger.
For analyses, scores of 1-2 were classified as frustration, while scores of 3-4 were classified as anger.

Critically, anger (scores 3 and 4) required explicit linguistic evidence of hostility, aggressive blame, threats, or emotional escalation, whereas frustration included expressions of impatience, irritation, or exasperation without these features.
Ratings were based on linguistic evidence of affect in context.

Although routine directives and prohibitions were not considered sufficient evidence of frustration, repeated prohibitions or requests could indicate possible frustration (score 1), particularly when suggesting impatience, urgency, or repeated blocked effort.
Fear.
Fear encompassed expressions of anxiety, worry, apprehension, alarm, or concern about actual or anticipated harm, danger, or unwanted outcomes.
Speech was rated on a 0-2 scale:0 = no fear,1 = possible or mild fear, and2 = clear fear.
Evidence included explicit references to fear as well as indirect expressions of concern, such as warnings about potential harm (e.g., "Be careful, you're going to get hurt!").
Fear-related discussions involving other people, hypothetical situations, or media content could also be coded.
However, neutral descriptions of potentially dangerous situations were not considered sufficient evidence of fear.
Sadness included expressions of emotional hurt, disappointment, loneliness, grief, loss, or sorrow.
Speech was rated on a 0-2 scale:0 = no sadness,1 = possible or mild sadness, and2 = clear sadness.
References to crying, loss, or sadness in others could also contribute to ratings, with ambiguous expressions generally receiving a score of 1.
Physical discomfort, tiredness, or general negativity alone were not considered sufficient evidence of sadness.
We coded seven categories of everyday activities: mealtimes, play, reading, music/singing, caregiving routines, sleep, and media.
Categories were not mutually exclusive, and multiple activities could be coded within the same 30-second segment when supported by the transcript.
Coding was based on linguistic evidence of activities, including descriptions, discussions, or indications of ongoing activities, as detailed below.

Because activity annotations were based on transcripts rather than direct observations of behavior they should be interpreted as transcript-based estimates of concurrent activity rather than direct behavioral observations.

Across human-human rating pairs, Cohen's kappa values were .607 for mealtimes, .500 for play, .845 for reading, .796 for music/singing, .698 for caregiving routines, .750 for sleep, and .325 for media, indicating acceptable agreement between our human coders.

Among human-GPT, pooled human-GPT precision for the 30-second segments was .825 for mealtimes, .700 for play, .775 for reading, .825 for music/singing, .800 for caregiving routines, .875 for sleep, and .800 for media (see SM11 for complete results).
Included talk that referenced eating, drinking, meal preparation, or related conversations about food consumption ("pass me a fork").
Mealtime activities were coded separately from general caregiving routines.
Play.

Included talk referencing toys, games, drawing, coloring, and outdoor or playground activities, as well as playful interactions with caregivers, siblings, or other children (i.e. playful or silly speech, e.g.
"I'm a carrot, no, you're a carrot").
Reading.
Included reading aloud, discussions of books or reading, and other references to ongoing reading activities.
To distinguish reading from other media, coders used linguistic features characteristic of written text (e.g. the phrase "she said" at the end of a speech quote).
Included transcriptions of singing, songs, and other musical vocal activities, as well as explicit references to music or singing.
Rhythmic, patterned vocal repetition could indicate singing even without identifiable lyrics, whereas ordinary conversational repetition was not sufficient.
Coders did not distinguish between music/signing from media vs human-generated.
Included text indicating bedtime and nap routines, i.e. preparations for sleeping and attempts to settle a child to sleep or back to sleep.

References indicating an anticipated or ongoing sleep routine were included, whereas general discussions of sleep unrelated to a current or upcoming routine ("she's been sleeping so badly this week") were excluded.
Caregiving routines.

Included speech referencing everyday child-directed care activities such as dressing, hygiene, toileting, bathing, and transitions associated with leaving the house (e.g., putting on shoes, gathering belongings, or getting into a car seat).
Coding required evidence of an identifiable caregiving activity rather than isolated instructions or ambiguous interactions.
Household chores unrelated to childcare were excluded.
Caregiving associated exclusively with meals or sleep was classified under those more specific categories.
Included text-based evidence of television, videos, tablets, phones, or other electronic media use, including speech originating from media.

When media content depicted activities such as play, eating, or caregiving, these activities were not coded unless there was independent evidence that they were also occurring in the child's immediate environment.
All Analyses were conducted in R.
Descriptive analyses.
Descriptives summarized participant demographic characteristics, LENA audio recording duration, maternal mental health scores and child temperament.
Affect and activity categories were summarized for each family using frequency and rate per hour considering all bins where speech was automatically detected.
Affect and activity distributions.
The overall distributions of affect and activity categories were examined using the raw count (Figure 2) or percentage of speechcontaining segments assigned to each category (for all analyses).

text.text: Segments labeled as None were retained in the denominator when calculating the prevalence of each affect or activity category.
Associations between affect and activity were examined by comparing the occurrence of predicted affect categories in segments that also contained predictions for specific activity contexts.
Differences in positive affect and negative affect across activity contexts were tested using two-sided, paired family-level t-tests with Benjamini-Hochberg (B-H) correction for multiple comparisons.
Positive affect included enjoyment, and negative affect had frustration, anger, sadness, and fear.
Between-sample comparisons of family-level proportions used Welch's t-tests, with BH correction across all emotions and activities separately.
Activity-affect associations.

We used multilevel mixed-effects logistic regression models to examine associations between everyday activities and emotional speech, separately for the infant (n = 70), toddler (n = 51), and child (n = 38) samples, and including sample interactions to estimate sample-specific associations.
Models predicted the presence or absence of affect in each 30-second speech segment from activity, distinguishing within-family and between-family associations.

To separate these effects, we included both a within-family predictor (the binary activity indicator centered around each family's mean proportion of segments containing that activity) and a between-family predictor (the family's mean proportion of segments containing that activity).

Thus, within-family effects captured differences in emotional speech when a given activity was present versus absent, whereas between-family effects captured associations between families' overall activity prevalence and emotional speech.

Models also included child age at recording centered within sample, sample group, interactions of sample group with two activity predictors (within and between), and a random intercept for each child.
We conducted modeling for two affects (frustration and enjoyment) with eight activities.
Between-family odds ratios were in per 10% increase in activity prevalence.
For visualization, we generated model-predicted probabilities of emotional speech.
Within-family predictions compared segments with and without each activity, holding family activity proportions at their sample means.
Between-family predictions varied activity proportions from the 5th to 95th percentile within each sample, holding withinfamily deviations at zero.
Predictions were calculated at the sample mean age, with random intercepts set to zero, and 95% Wald confidence intervals were estimated and transformed to probabilities.

Statistical significance was assessed using two-sided Wald tests of sample-specific coefficients against zero, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction across 96 comparisons (two emotions × eight activities × three samples × two effects).
Affect-Child and Parent Characteristics.
Associations between maternal mental health and child temperament with family emotional speech were examined using Pearson correlations.
The maternal mental health variables were anxiety and depression scores from each sample.
The child temperament variables were Orienting/Regulation, Negative Affectivity and Surgency.
The emotional speech outcomes included the rate per hour of the full LENA recording time for each relevant affect category.
Analyses controlled for child age.
Statistical significance was set at p < .05.
